children.text: A waterfall about 98m high in the Campangga valley of Barili town on Cebu's west coast, considered the island's tallest. It's just a few minutes' walk from the parking area, and the pool below the lower falls is great for bamboo rafting and swimming, making it a good family day trip.
Mantayupan Falls sits in Barangay Campangga, in the town of Barili, about
southwest of Cebu City. The main cascade stands about
tall, said to be the tallest waterfall on Cebu, and below it a smaller falls about
high feeds a wide pool. Locals also call it Ambakan, meaning "a place to jump from," and both names appear together on the entrance signboard.
For a long time it was a hidden valley known only to villagers, but a road was built in

when the Cebu I Electric Cooperative (CEBECO) put up a small hydropower facility using the falls' water. The valley's water still irrigates the rice paddies downstream and turns the power plant today, and since

a village cooperative has managed admission and facilities. As a result, it has fewer commercial developments than other famous waterfalls, and the atmosphere of a valley ringed by thick forest and cliffs remains well preserved.

Its biggest advantage is accessibility. Buy your ticket at the parking area, walk down the steps, and you reach the lower falls in under a minute; cross the hanging bridge over the valley and walk just a few minutes more to look straight up at the 98m main cascade. Unlike Kawasan Falls or canyoning, which require a long trek, this is an easy trip for children and older visitors alike.

It's an easy day trip from Cebu City, and works well as a stop on a southern Cebu loop combining it with Moalboal on the west coast or Kawasan Falls to the south. Recommended for families, groups of friends, and photographers who'd rather spread out a picnic and splash around in a quiet valley than fight crowds at a busy tourist spot.

Cross the hanging bridge into the valley and the main falls appears, a slender ribbon of water dropping a long way between green cliffs. Near the end of the rainy season, the flow swells and spray reaches all the way to the viewpoint.

blocks.title: Bamboo rafting at the lower falls

children.text: At the pool in front of the lower falls, about
high, you can rent a bamboo raft (around
) and paddle right up to the base of the falls. Taking photos while the spray hits you is this spot's signature experience.

blocks.title: The hanging bridge across the valley

children.text: The hanging bridge strung over the valley between the two falls is a photo spot that takes in the forest and waterfall in one frame. It sways, so avoid letting too many people cross at once.

blocks.title: Swimming and diving in the pool

children.text: The pool at the lower falls is fairly deep, so swimmers rent a life vest (around
). Some people jump from a rock about
4m
high, where the caretaker allows it.
You can rent tables and huts around the falls, a good spot to spread out roast chicken or lechon bought at Barili market and spend half a day.
Arrive right at opening time and you'll have the place nearly to yourself, with sunlight slanting into the valley for the most beautiful shots of the falls and forest.
Sta. Ana Church in central Barili is an old Spanish-era church, a nice stop on the way to the falls. Around its patron saint's feast day in late
July
, the town holds the Panumod Festival.

From Cebu City's South Bus Terminal, take a Ceres bus heading toward Bato or Moalboal via Barili. The route that crosses the mountains from Carcar to the west coast passes through Barili, taking about
2 hours–2 hours 30 minutes
, with fares around
for an air-conditioned bus.

It helps to tell the conductor in advance that you're getting off in Barili town (at the market or in front of the 7-Eleven). A V-hire shared van departing from near the South Terminal also takes about
2 hours
to Barili.
It's about
3.7km
from Barili town to the falls entrance. A habal-habal (motorbike taxi) takes about
10 minutes
, with a negotiated one-way fare of around
It can be hard to flag down a habal-habal on the way back, so it's best to agree on a pickup time with the driver or get their contact number.
Drive along the southern coastal road from Cebu City to Carcar, then over the Carcar–Barili mountain road, and it takes about
2 hours–2 hours 30 minutes
. There's a parking area at the falls entrance with a fee of about
Chartering a car with driver for the day costs about
, and it's easy to build an itinerary that also takes in Carcar, Moalboal, and Kawasan Falls.
From Moalboal, take a northbound Cebu City-bound bus and get off in Barili — about
1 hour
, with fares around
Coming straight from Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB), budget about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
by Grab or chartered vehicle.
The dry season from
December
through
May

, when the water is clear and the valley paths aren't slippery, is best. During this period the pool turns a turquoise color that photographs beautifully, and you can enjoy rafting and swimming with confidence. In peak summer,
March–May
, however, the flow can drop and the main falls may thin out.
From
June
to
November

is the rainy season, when the flow increases dramatically and the falls look most dramatic, but the water often runs muddy, and swimming is sometimes restricted for safety after heavy rain. In some years Cebu is affected by typhoons in
October–December
, so check the forecast. Time-wise, right after opening at
7–9 AM
is quietest, while weekend and holiday afternoons draw many local families. Temperatures run around
year-round, though the valley stays cool with plenty of shade.

Since Mantayupan Falls is usually visited as a day trip from Cebu City, most travelers base themselves in Cebu City or Mactan. The valley's management cooperative runs simple rooms near the falls for about
a night, though the facilities are basic. If you're planning several days around southern Cebu, it's more convenient to stay at Panagsama Beach in Moalboal, about
1 hour
by car, where a guesthouse runs about
and a beach resort about

At the falls entrance there are small eateries and stalls selling grilled meat, rice, and drinks, but the choices are limited. Like local families do, it's worth buying roast chicken lechon manok or puso (rice wrapped in woven palm leaves) and fruit at Barili market to eat at a hut. Carcar, a stop on the way back, is famous for crispy fried pork rind chicharon and the rice cracker ampao, and in Cebu City you shouldn't miss Cebu-style whole roast pig, lechon.
Entrance fees, rafts, and habal-habal rides are all cash only, so bring plenty of small bills. There's no ATM near the falls.
Opening hours generally run from about
6–7 AM
to around
5 PM
, and swimming may be restricted depending on weather conditions, so check the official page before visiting.
Rocks and steps are wet and slippery, so wear aqua shoes or strap sandals.
Bring a dry bag, a change of clothes, and a towel so you can travel back comfortably after getting soaked on the raft.
If you want to fly a drone over the main falls, satellite signal is weak inside the valley, so it's better to launch from the open area near the parking lot.
If you're doing a southern Cebu loop, visiting Mantayupan early in the morning and Moalboal in the afternoon makes for a natural route.
Return buses thin out around sunset, so it's safer to be back in Barili town before
4 PM
After heavy rain, the valley's water can rise suddenly and turn muddy, so if the caretaker stops swimming, you must comply.
The pool at the lower falls is deep in the middle. If you're not a confident swimmer, be sure to wear a life vest, and children should be watched closely by a guardian.
Only jump from the rocks at spots the caretaker allows, after checking the water depth and the rocks below.
Limit the number of people on the hanging bridge at once, and don't run or shake it.
Mosquitoes are common in the valley, so bring insect repellent.
Since the falls' water is used for power generation and irrigating rice paddies, avoid using soap or shampoo and don't litter.
